anchors.paper_title: Electroencephalography, pupillometry, and behavioral evidence for locus coeruleus-noradrenaline system related tonic hyperactivity in older adults
anchors.reason: Same authors (Kim, Morales, Senior, Mather) report the older-adult EEG passive/active auditory oddball study with threat-of-shock arousal manipulation, matching this HeartBEAM dataset's conditions.

metadata.methods_description: Five-minute eyes-open and eyes-closed resting state recordings and passive and active auditory oddball tasks (standard, target and distractor tones) were collected in a control condition and a shock-threat condition. Event markers code the task, condition, and trial phase.

citation_details.title: DeeperBrain: A Neuro-Grounded EEG Foundation Model Towards Universal BCI
citation_details.author: Jiquan Wang, Sha Zhao, Yang-Xuan Zhou, Yiming Kang, Shi-Jian Li, Gang Pan
citation_details.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models hold significant promise for universal Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs). However, existing approaches often rely on end-to-end fine-tuning and exhibit limited efficacy under frozen-probing protocols, lacking the intrinsic universality required for broad generalization. This limitation stems from adapting general-purpose sequence architectures that overlook the biophysical and dynamical principles of neural activity. To bridge this gap, we propose DeeperBrain, a neuro-grounded foundation model integrating domain-specific inductive biases into its model design and learning objectives. Architecturally, DeeperBrain incorporates a volume conduction-aware channel encoding to model spatial mixing via 3D geometry, and a neurodynamics-aware temporal encoding capturing slow adaptations using oscillatory and exponential bases. citation_details.title: ERP-FM: A Foundation Model for Universal ERP Analysis
citation_details.author: Yi-He Wang, Bo Chen, Tai-Da Li, Yu-Jun Yan, Rui Yin, Xiang Zhang
citation_details.abstract: Foundation models have recently shown strong potential for learning generalizable EEG representations, yet their effectiveness for event-related potential (ERP) analysis remains unclear. In this work, we investigate two fundamental questions: 1) can foundation-model learning benefit ERP analysis, and what limits the transfer of existing EEG foundation models to ERP tasks? 2) can the complementary advantages of single-trial and averaged-trial ERP be integrated into a unified training pipeline? To study these questions, we curate a large-scale ERP corpus comprising 1,517,157 single-trial ERPs from 3,696 subjects across 38 datasets and 18 paradigms. Leveraging this corpus, we introduce ERP-FM, to the best of our knowledge, the first foundation model specifically developed for ERP representation learning. citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai C
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.
